\chapter{Morning}
\label{ch:la-morning}
\hlchaptermodality{31}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say morning in Latin with māne, and keep it apart from manus, the hand.}

Say māne, recover it inside dē māne and mañana, and keep long-ā mānus apart from short-a manus, the hand.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[māne]{māne — the word already hiding inside \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow,\textquotedblright{} in four languages}

\label{lesson:LA-C31-mane}



\begin{quote}
You've already met this word once, without a lesson of its own — buried inside the very phrase that replaced \emph{crās} across half the Romance family. Time to meet it directly.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: māne — \textquotedblleft{}morning,\textquotedblright{} an indeclinable word}]
\textbf{Māne} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{morning, early}\textquotedblright{} — is an \textbf{indeclinable} neuter noun (and adverb): unlike \emph{diēs} or \emph{nox}, it never changes its ending, no matter its grammatical role. You've already met it once, inside \textbf{dē māne} (\textquotedblleft{}in the morning,\textquotedblright{} Chapter 25) — the exact phrase that \textbf{French}'s \emph{demain}, \textbf{Italian}'s \emph{domani}, and \textbf{Catalan}'s \emph{demà} all independently rebuilt as their new word for \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow,\textquotedblright{} abandoning \emph{crās}. \textbf{Spanish}'s \emph{mañana} took a related but distinct path: built directly on \textbf{māne} itself, without the \emph{dē}- (Vulgar Latin \emph{*maneāna}) — the same root, one step closer to the source.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Māne traces to \textbf{mānus}, an archaic Latin adjective meaning \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{good}.\textquotedblright{} Watch the vowel length carefully: this is a \textbf{completely different} word from the everyday \textbf{manus} (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{hand},\textquotedblright{} short \emph{a}) — same spelling once macrons are dropped, unrelated meaning, a genuine false friend. From that \textquotedblleft{}good\textquotedblright{} root comes \textbf{mātūrus} (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{ripe, timely, early}\textquotedblright{}), the direct source of English \textbf{mature} — and \textbf{mātūtīnus} (\textquotedblleft{}of the morning,\textquotedblright{} tied to \textbf{Matūta}, the Roman goddess of dawn), which gives English, via Old French \emph{matines}/\emph{matin}, both \textbf{matins} (\textquotedblleft{}morning prayers\textquotedblright{}) \textbf{and} \textbf{matinee} (\textquotedblleft{}afternoon performance\textquotedblright{}) — the same root splitting into two very different senses of \textquotedblleft{}a scheduled morning-adjacent thing.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}māne\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}morning,\textquotedblright{} already met inside dē māne
  \item the false-friend warning — mānus \textquotedblleft{}good\textquotedblright{} (long ā) vs. manus \textquotedblleft{}hand\textquotedblright{} (short a)
  \item the English cousins — mature, matins, matinee, all from the same root as māne
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where did you already meet \textbf{māne} before this lesson? (Inside \textbf{dē māne}, \textquotedblleft{}in the morning,\textquotedblright{} Chapter 25 — source of French \emph{demain}, Italian \emph{domani}, and Catalan \emph{demà}.) Did Spanish \emph{mañana} come from \emph{dē māne} too? (\textbf{Not quite} — it was built directly on \emph{māne} alone, without the \emph{dē}-.) Is māne's root \emph{mānus} the same word as \emph{manus}, \textquotedblleft{}hand\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{No} — a false friend; \emph{mānus} \textquotedblleft{}good\textquotedblright{} has a long ā, \emph{manus} \textquotedblleft{}hand\textquotedblright{} a short a.) What two very different English words both trace to māne's \textquotedblleft{}good\textquotedblright{} root, via \emph{mātūtīnus}? (\textbf{Matins} and \textbf{matinee}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
